cold-open.script: Start with a prediction. When the level changes, who will survive: the human player, the agent trained on that player, or neither? A precise answer should wait. First we need demonstrations, a model, unseen test levels, and a fair comparison. That sequence separates a game impression from research evidence. Keep your opening vote. At the end, compare it with the measured result and explain why your expectation did or did not match the evidence.

mission.script: The workshop has five connected phases. You play, train, hand over control, try to break the agent on unseen levels, and defend a bounded conclusion. Every action in the first phase becomes evidence used later. This is one continuous investigation rather than two disconnected coding labs. You leave with a gameplay CSV if you choose to export it, a trained browser policy, a controlled-experiment receipt, code you can read, and a short research claim.

We do not bypass access controls or anti-cheat systems, and we do not ask for a camera, microphone, account, or identity. Gameplay remains in the browser unless the student deliberately exports a local CSV. This boundary makes automatic play legitimate, inspectable, and reproducible. It also keeps the exciting moment when software visibly takes control.

rules.script: Every decision step begins with a survival reward of positive zero point zero two. If a coin is collected on that step, add ten; if a hazard is hit, subtract twelve. That is why the CSV usually shows zero point zero two. A coin row is ten point zero two, and a hazard row is negative eleven point nine eight. Every one hundred milliseconds, the browser records the current sensor state and the action LEFT, STAY, or RIGHT. Doing nothing is not missing data; STAY is a real action label. Reward is the immediate outcome recorded in the row. The action is the imitation-learning label, and the displayed score is the running game total.

row.script: This slide is the key translation from an animated game to a research table. Begin with the picture on the left, not with the abbreviations. The suffix d x means delta x, a horizontal offset relative to the player. A negative obstacle d x places the nearest hazard to the left, zero means the same lane, and a positive value places it to the right. Obstacle distance and coin distance measure how far forward the nearest object is. Zero means very near; one means far away or absent. These values are normalized, so they are not screen pixels or meters. Now read the complete row at the bottom. Four measurements form the state. RIGHT is the human action and therefore the training label. Positive zero point zero two is the immediate survival reward that followed. One row is one decision, not one entire game.

agent-loop.script: An agent repeats a loop: observe the state, compare it with experience, choose an action, act, and observe the changed world. The word agent matters because an action changes the next input. Moving right can collect a coin, avoid a hazard, and place the player in a new situation for the next decision. Later work can replace imitation learning with reinforcement learning that optimizes long-term reward. For this experience class, imitation is faster, more stable, and easier to inspect.

knn.script: To make k nearest neighbors visible, we temporarily project the demonstration rows onto two features. The real game uses four. Pink circles are LEFT examples. Gold squares are STAY examples. Teal triangles are RIGHT examples. The black star is a new state the agent has never labeled. Set k equal to nine. The dashed circle encloses the nine closest demonstrations. Neighbor one. Neighbor two. Neighbor three. Neighbor four. Neighbor five. Neighbor six. Neighbor seven. Neighbor eight. Neighbor nine. Now vote. Among these nine, LEFT has two examples, STAY has three, and RIGHT has four. After inverse-distance weighting, the shares are about seventeen percent LEFT, thirty-three percent STAY, and fifty percent RIGHT. RIGHT wins and becomes the next action. The production policy repeats the same idea in four dimensions and also balances action classes.

code-core.script: Before reading individual lines, step back and follow the complete agent loop. Game Frame is the current world: the player's lane, coins, and hazards. Observe means environment.js converts that world into four numeric sensors. Predict means policy.js compares those numbers with demonstration rows, combines the nearest weighted votes, and chooses an action. Action sends LEFT, STAY, or RIGHT back to the game. Environment applies that move, advances the objects, calculates the reward, and creates the next frame. Repeat means app.js coordinates this loop every one hundred milliseconds while it also updates the display, records demonstrations, and exports the CSV. Now connect those stages to the four files in the GitHub source. environment.js defines the world, sensors, rewards, seeded levels, and expert labels. policy.js contains trainKnn and the live weighted k-NN predictor shown here. app.js connects the controls, animation, agent loop, receipts, CSV export, and local run history. experiment.js runs the controlled one-seed-versus-twelve-seed evaluation on unseen levels. The editor now contains the complete policy.js file: its distance helper, input checks, class balancing, neighbor search, weighted probabilities, decision receipt, and exports for both the browser and Node tests. After this overview, use Explain complete policy dot J S line by line for the separate code walkthrough.

code-walk.script: Read the complete file as six testable responsibilities, not as one sixty-four-line block. The wrapper creates a safe module boundary, and squaredDistance defines exactly what nearby means. trainKnn validates its inputs, counts LEFT, STAY, and RIGHT examples, and gives rarer classes more weight. The returned model keeps rows, k, and counts as an inspectable training receipt. Inside predict, the code measures every demonstration, sorts by distance, keeps the nearest k, and accumulates class-balanced inverse-distance votes. It then normalizes those votes into probabilities, chooses the winning action, and returns the evidence behind the decision: probabilities, raw votes, neighbors, and nearest distance. Finally, the export lines make the same tested functions available to Node and the browser. If every demonstration says STAY, inspect counts and data coverage before blaming the syntax.

lab-takeover.script: Now watch the real handoff. First train the local weighted-neighbor policy and press AI Takeover; the policy drives without keyboard input using balanced starter demonstrations plus your capped personal examples. Next choose AI Unseen. It runs the policy on a held-out level sequence. Then choose Human Unseen and drive the same held-out seed order yourself. Those human test actions are evaluation only and never become training rows. The local comparison panel records completed runs, best score, and average separately for Human, AI Takeover, Human Unseen, and AI Unseen. Use the two unseen rows for the fairest human-versus-agent comparison. One important boundary: the Generalization Test farther down the page is a separate deterministic benchmark with fixed training and test seeds. Live unseen runs change the score panel, but they do not change that fixed benchmark.

research-question.script: The classroom research question asks whether more training-level diversity improves performance on levels the agent has never seen. The comparison fixes the data budget at two hundred forty rows. One condition uses demonstrations from one training seed, and the other spreads the same number of rows across twelve seeds. Both conditions use the same four features, weighted-neighbor model, k value, and twenty unseen test seeds. The primary outcome is accuracy on six hundred expert-labeled actions.

quiz-fair.script: Quick check. Suppose the twelve-seed agent receives two thousand four hundred rows while the one-seed agent receives only two hundred forty. Can a score difference be attributed to diversity? No. Training amount also changed, so diversity and quantity are confounded. A controlled comparison gives both agents the same number of rows and changes only seed diversity. Controls do not make an experiment perfect. They make one explanation more testable by preventing an obvious second variable from changing at the same time.

lab-experiment.script: Lab three runs the fair test directly in the browser. The result is computed when the button is pressed; it is not a number written into the lesson. In our reproducible classroom run, the one-seed policy achieved ninety-one point zero percent held-out action accuracy, while the twelve-seed policy achieved eighty-four point three percent. Mean game scores were one hundred five point zero and sixty-six point seven. More diversity did not automatically win under a fixed row budget. Spreading rows across levels may improve coverage while reducing the density of examples for each situation. That mechanism is a hypothesis, not a proven cause. Repeat across training draws, vary the data budget, and compare another policy model before making a general claim.

claim.script: Write the result with four parts: scope, measured comparison, limitation, and next test. A strong sentence reports both accuracies and says that each condition had two hundred forty rows. It then limits the finding to one three-lane game and one neighbor-model setting. If the result contradicts your prediction, report it exactly. A surprising result is valuable when the comparison is fair and the next experiment is clear.

public-backing.script: The classroom question mirrors established game-AI research. Procgen uses sixteen procedurally generated game-like environments to study sample efficiency and generalization. GVGAI provides an open framework for agents that must act across many games, including games they did not train on. The NetHack Learning Dataset contains human and symbolic-bot trajectories. These resources establish that generalization, player trajectories, and agent behavior are valuable research areas. Public access still requires careful license and provenance documentation.

open-data-question.script: Next we move from an open environment to a real open dataset. SkillCraft One contains three thousand three hundred ninety-five StarCraft Two player records and is licensed Creative Commons Attribution Four Point Zero. The target is League Index at least five, from Diamond through Professional. There are one thousand five hundred seventeen records in this class and one thousand eight hundred seventy-eight in leagues one through four. Our compact condition uses four interpretable sensors: actions per minute, hotkey selection, action latency, and number of perception-action cycles. The extension uses all fifteen behavioral telemetry features. The research question is how much predictive performance is lost with four sensors instead of fifteen. Same players, target, preprocessing, logistic-regression model, and five folds; only the sensor set changes.

same-pipeline.script: The game is our first sandbox, not the final destination. The same research pipeline can guide a warehouse robot, a wellness study, sports analysis, or a mobility system. Across these domains, the loop remains recognizable: observe a situation, represent it as data, learn a pattern, test unseen cases, measure outcomes, and improve the next experiment. What transfers is not a game-control trick. It is the ability to define evidence, hold comparisons fair, inspect failures, respect domain boundaries, and support every conclusion with a result another person can check.

exit.script: The bot played, but the student did the research. The student created labels, read the code, inspected the model, designed a controlled comparison, and decided where the evidence stopped. The most useful exit question is not whether the agent looked intelligent. It is what you would inspect first after a failure: data coverage, sensors, model behavior, code, or experiment design. You can now carry that complete research pipeline into a new domain: begin with an observable question, build a fair test, and let evidence determine what you are ready to claim.
